subject: giraffe
pitch: A young reticulated giraffe. Chestnut patches outlined by bright cream lines all over its body and neck, a short mane of stiff brown hair down the neck, two fuzzy ossicones with black tufts on top, big ears, long lashes, a long dark tongue just peeking out, and slender legs fading to cream above the hooves.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a young giraffe model using the SDK, working out realistic proportions like a shoulder height around 3.2 meters, and sketching the builder API structure I'll use to construct it piece by piece.

For the giraffe itself, I'm mapping the anatomy to the builder's tools: a barrel-like body, four leg chains with proper joints down to the hooves, a long neck chain angled up and forward, a separate head joint with a jaw, and ossicones built from small rods or spikes topped with dark tufted caps.

I'm now working out the actual coordinate system and skeleton layout — forward is +Z, up is +Y, and I'm placing the pelvis as the root joint near the body's center, then figuring out realistic proportions for body length, shoulder height, and leg length so the giraffe's frame feels right before I start positioning the limbs.

For the spine, I'm building a chain of three points curving gently from pelvis to withers, matching the number of segment names to the number of spans between points so the chain API doesn't throw an error. Now I'm double-checking how parenting works for the chain's root joint relative to the pelvis.

To keep things simpler and reduce the risk of API mismatches, I'm deciding to build the spine with explicit individual joints rather than relying on the chain helper, while still using chains for the legs and neck.

I'm sketching out the joint hierarchy: a root "pelvis" joint, then a "chest" joint parented to it, each with positions and orientation hints, planning to keep the structure straightforward with simple directional defaults.

Now I'm working out the neck chain geometry — defining base and tip positions angled steeply upward to capture a giraffe-like neck, with path points curving from the chest toward the head and tapering the radius from thick at the base to narrower near the top.

So span joints sit at the start of each span -- neck1 at p0, neck2 at p1 -- and the final path point p2 is left without its own joint, becoming the tip where the head attaches.

I'll name three joints so the tip gets one too: neck1, neck2, neck3, with neck3 as the tip joint carrying the neck role. The head joint parents to neck3 and sits at roughly [0, 3.35, 1.15], tilted slightly forward-down to match the giraffe's posture, built around that same joint position.

For the head geometry, I'm working in model-space coordinates throughout, attaching parts to the head bone so they inherit its pose. I'm shaping the muzzle as a capsule running from roughly [0, 3.35, 1.5] to [0, 3.25, 1.85] with a radius around 0.11 to get that elongated giraffe snout.

Still building out the head and jaw...

Now I'm placing the two ossicones as rods running from the forehead base up to tips near the top of the skull, giving them a tan/fawn color and tying them to the head bone for proper weighting.

For the tufted ends, I'm adding a small dark brown sphere at each ossicone tip to represent the fuzzy knob. Then I'm moving on to the ears, planning to build them as flattened leaf-shaped slabs using a set of points positioned on either side of the head.

Eye as a small dark sphere, with lashes made from thin radiating rods rather than textured cards—several per eye, pointed upward and outward, radius around 0.006 for fine detail. Simpler than cards but should read as lashes at this scale.

For the mane, I'm considering stiff dark brown spikes along the neck's back line instead of textured hair cards, since cards require UV-mapped geometry and a texture source. Using spike cones placed along frames from the neck chain, iterating with b.along to position each spike on the back side of the neck pointing outward.

Since a SweepPoint frame converts to a point, I can pass it directly as the spike's base, with angle 0 giving the dorsal side where the mane should sit, tilted slightly back along the neck's curve. For the actual neck geometry I'll call the sweep function with the chain and radius to build the surface.

For the taper, I'm using a two-value radius array for linear interpolation, matching how the rod/capsule geometry handles tapering ends. Then for the coloring I'll apply a patch pattern over a cream base with chestnut patches layered on top to get the body's coloring.

For the legs, I want them fading from a patterned chestnut top to solid cream near the hooves, so I'm setting up a gradient between a leg-patch color and cream running from the upper leg down to the hoof position.

For the hooves, I'm adding them as a separate dark brown part—a simple capsule or cylinder shape attached at the base of each leg.

Now I'm working out the legs as joint chains, with hip joints positioned on each side and giraffe-appropriate proportions, front legs angled slightly forward from hip to hoof.

I'll use four points per leg to get three spans (upper, knee, ankle) plus a tip joint for the hoof, naming them so the hoof joint sits at the path's end for contact detection. Working through the giraffe's leg path geometry now...

Straight polyline segments should work fine for nearly-vertical legs, and I'll sweep a tapered tube radius along the chain. I'm planning the joint naming convention now, using side-prefixed labels like "frontL1, frontL2, frontL3, frontLhoof" to keep them valid identifiers while staying systematic across all four legs.

Now I'm shifting to the body itself, planning to loft it as a barrel-shaped torso from several stations running from rump to chest, each with its own position, width, and height to capture the giraffe's distinctive body shape before it transitions into the neck.

With pelvis at t near 0 and chest near t near 1 for the bone spans, that should work fine. I'm considering bumping the loft's sides from the default 8 up to 10 for a less blocky look, and I still need to figure out how to paint color patches over the body.
